sections.title: 1. What DAI Is About & How the Course Works
sections.description: Understand the four core pillars of Développement d'Applications Internet (DAI) and how theory, labs, and practical works fit together.

blocks.title: The Four Pillars of DAI
blocks.content:
The Internet runs on programs talking to each other. In **Développement d'Applications Internet (DAI)**, you learn to build those programs from the ground up—not by treating the network as magic, but by understanding every layer from raw bytes to production web infrastructure.

By the end of the semester, you will master four interconnected skills:

1. **Network Programming (I/O, Encodings, TCP & UDP):** Build client-server applications using the Socket API, starting from raw byte streams and character encodings.
2. **Application-Level Protocols:** Understand how real Internet protocols work (`SMTP`, `SSH`, `HTTP`, …) and then design and implement your own custom protocol.
3. **Web Infrastructures:** Deploy your applications the way they run in production using **reverse proxies**, **load balancers**, and **sticky sessions**.
4. **Technical Documentation:** Read specifications accurately and write clear `README`s and technical reports—the meta-skill behind all engineering collaboration.

Along the way, you will adopt industry-standard tooling: **Git & GitHub**, **Docker** (introduced in Chapter 05), **Maven**, and the **Unix terminal**.

blocks.title: How the Course Works: Rhythm, Communication & Callouts
blocks.content:
Each week combines a short **cours** (theory) and a **labo** (practice—where most of your learning happens). Keep these operational rules in mind:

- **Chapters:** Contain the core theory, exercises with solutions, and collapsible **Go further** boxes for the curious. Evaluations only cover the **core content**.
- **Practical Works (PW):** Three multi-week group projects that anchor theory in real applications. You choose your own subject (validated by the teaching team).
- **Communication:** Everything happens on **GitHub Discussions** (questions, answers, announcements). There is **no Cyberlearn** and **no Teams**.
- **Languages:** Course material is in **English** (the language of software engineering), while classes and evaluations are in **French**.

### How to Read Chapter Callouts

| Callout Type | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Note** | Worth knowing, even when skimming |
| **Tip** | Optional helper or shortcut |
| **Important** | Essential requirement needed to succeed |
| **Warning** | Risk ahead—proceed carefully |
| **Caution** | Negative consequences if ignored (e.g., data/permission issues) |

sections.title: 2. Grading Formula & Responsible AI Policy
sections.description: Explore how your final grade is weighted across TE1, TE2, and PW, and understand the ground rules for using AI assistants.

blocks.title: The DAI Grading Formula
blocks.content:
There is **no exam session** in DAI—everything happens during the semester. Your final grade is computed as:

$$\text{final grade} = \underbrace{(\text{TE1} \times 0.4 + \text{TE2} \times 0.6)}_{\text{cours (80\%)}} \times 0.8 + \underbrace{\text{PW}}_{\text{labo (20\%)}} \times 0.2$$

Where:
- **TE1:** Mid-term evaluation (effective weight: $0.4 \times 0.8 = 32\%$ of the final grade).
- **TE2:** Final evaluation (effective weight: $0.6 \times 0.8 = 48\%$ of the final grade).
- **PW:** Average of your **three** practical works, each graded on its report and deliverables using published rubrics (effective weight: $20\%$ of the final grade).

> **Non-Example (Common Mistake):** Treating PW as "only 20%" and neglecting reports. On a 1.0–6.0 Swiss grading scale, losing 2 points on PW costs $2.0 \times 0.2 = 0.4$ full grade points—often the difference between passing and failing. Similarly, TE2 alone carries nearly half ($48\%$) of your entire course grade!

blocks.title: AI Tools Policy: Understand, Don't Outsource
blocks.content:
AI assistants (GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude, …) are part of modern software engineering, and DAI takes a pragmatic stance: you may use them responsibly within school guidelines.

Three non-negotiable ground rules apply:

1. **Use AI to understand, not to bypass thinking:** Ask it to explain a compiler error, clarify a protocol concept, or compare two design approaches—never to generate a solution you do not comprehend.
2. **Line-by-line accountability:** You are accountable for everything you submit. **If you cannot explain your code line by line, it is not your code.**
3. **Evaluations have zero AI assistance:** Both TE1 and TE2 happen without AI. If you let an assistant do the learning during labs, the gap will show immediately during evaluations.

blocks.title: Practice: Compute the Target TE2 Score
blocks.instructions: Suppose a student has `te1 = 4.0` and `pw = 5.5`. They want a `targetGrade = 5.0`. Using the DAI grading formula `final = (te1 * 0.4 + te2 * 0.6) * 0.8 + pw * 0.2`, solve for `te2` and print the required TE2 grade formatted to 2 decimal places (`toFixed(2)`).
hints: First isolate the `cours` component by subtracting `pw * 0.2` from `targetGrade`, then dividing by `0.8`.
Next, isolate `te2` from `coursNeeded = te1 * 0.4 + te2 * 0.6` by subtracting `te1 * 0.4` and dividing by `0.6`.

sections.title: 3. OS Environment Setup: macOS, Linux & Windows (WSL2)
sections.description: Prepare a genuine Unix environment on your machine before Week 1, and understand why WSL2 filesystem boundaries matter.

blocks.title: Why Every OS Needs a Unix Shell
blocks.content:
Every command in DAI runs in a Unix terminal. How you get there depends on your OS (estimated setup time: ~30 min on macOS/Linux, 1–2 hours on Windows):

- **Linux:** You already have a native Unix shell and `apt` (or your distro's package manager). Skip straight to Terminal basics.
- **macOS:** Install **Homebrew** (https://brew.sh), the de-facto package manager for macOS (equivalent to Ubuntu's `apt`). After running the one-line installer, **run the "Next steps" commands** it prints so `brew` is added to your shell's `PATH`. Verify in a new terminal with `brew --version`.
- **Windows:** Install **WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux)** with **Ubuntu LTS**. PowerShell is used *only* for the Windows-side WSL setup steps; for the rest of the semester, every command runs inside the Ubuntu terminal.

> **Non-Example:** Git Bash, Cygwin, or MSYS2 are **not supported** in DAI. Only a real Linux environment via WSL2 behaves identically to production Linux servers and Docker containers.

blocks.title: Windows WSL2: File Locations & Defender Exclusion
blocks.content:
Understanding where files live in WSL2 prevents the #1 source of Windows student headaches:

1. **Ubuntu Home (`~` / `/home/<user>`):** When you open the Ubuntu terminal, you land in `/home/<user>`. **All your DAI projects must live here.**
2. **Seeing Windows from Ubuntu (`/mnt/`):** Windows drives are mounted under `/mnt/`, e.g., `C:\Users` is `/mnt/c/Users`.
3. **Seeing Ubuntu from Windows (`\\wsl.localhost\...`):** Windows File Explorer can view your Ubuntu home at `\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-<version>\home\<user>`.

> **Caution:** **Never manipulate project files from Windows File Explorer** (or store projects on `C:\`). Crossing the OS filesystem boundary causes Linux file permission corruption, line-ending bugs, and severe I/O slowdowns. Always use the Ubuntu terminal or IntelliJ.

### Mandatory Windows Defender Exclusion

Windows Defender scanning WSL2 virtual disk activity causes massive slowdowns and is a known blocker that prevents IntelliJ from detecting Java/Maven in WSL. Exclude your WSL path in an **Administrator PowerShell**:

```powershell
Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath '\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-<your-version>'
```

blocks.title: Annotated Windows WSL2 Setup Sequence
blocks.code:
# Run in Administrator PowerShell (Step 1)
wsl --install --no-distribution
# -> Reboot Windows, then run Step 2 in Admin PowerShell:
wsl --update --web-download
wsl --set-default-version 2
wsl --list --online
wsl --install --distribution Ubuntu-24.04
# Exclude WSL from Windows Defender
Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath '\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-24.04'
# Inside Ubuntu terminal: refresh catalog & upgrade packages
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

annotations.note: Installs the WSL2 kernel/platform first without a default distro so you can pick a versioned Ubuntu LTS.
Ensures WSL2 (real Linux kernel in lightweight VM) is the default rather than legacy WSL1.
Use a versioned LTS entry (e.g., Ubuntu-24.04 or Ubuntu-26.04), not the unversioned 'Ubuntu' entry.
Prevents Windows Defender from throttling WSL I/O or blocking IntelliJ's Java/Maven detection.
sudo runs as superuser (password typing is invisible!); apt update refreshes package metadata, apt upgrade installs updates.

sections.title: 4. Terminal Basics & Git Configuration
sections.description: Build muscle memory for essential Unix commands and configure Git & GitHub for the semester.

blocks.title: Essential Unix Terminal Commands
blocks.content:
You will live in the terminal this semester. Use `man <command>` whenever you want to inspect a command's manual.

| Command | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- |
| `pwd` | Print the current working directory |
| `ls` | List files and directories |
| `cd <dir>` / `cd ..` | Change directory / move to parent directory |
| `touch <file>` | Create an empty file |
| `mkdir <dir>` | Create a directory |
| `rm <file>` / `rm -r <dir>` | Remove a file / recursively remove a directory |
| `cp <src> <dst>` | Copy a file (add `-r` for directories) |
| `mv <src> <dst>` | Move or rename a file/directory |
| `cat <file>` | Print the entire contents of a file |
| `less <file>` / `more <file>` | Page through a file (`q` to quit) |
| `tail <file>` | Print the last lines (`-f` to follow live logs) |
| `exit` | Close the terminal session |

**Verification Challenge:** Create a directory, create a file inside it, list it, and delete both—without touching your mouse.

blocks.title: Practice: WSL2 Path Safety Validator
blocks.instructions: Write a Python function `is_safe_wsl_path(path)` that returns `True` if a project path is safely inside the Linux `/home/` directory (or uses `~`), and `False` if it is on a Windows mount (`/mnt/...`) or a Windows-style path (`C:\...` or `\\wsl.localhost\...`). Run the code to verify all test cases pass.
blocks.starter_code:
def is_safe_wsl_path(path: str) -> bool:
    # TODO: Return True only if path starts with '/home/' or '~'
    pass

tests = [
    ("/home/alice/dai-lab01", True),
    ("~/projects/smtp-client", True),
    ("/mnt/c/Users/alice/dai-lab01", False),
    ("C:\\Users\\alice\\dai-lab01", False),
]

for p, expected in tests:
    result = is_safe_wsl_path(p)
    assert result == expected, f"Failed for {p}: got {result}, expected {expected}"

hints: Check `path.startswith('/home/')` for absolute Linux home paths.
Also allow `path == '~'` or `path.startswith('~/')` for home shorthand.

blocks.title: Git Installation, Identity & GitHub Account
blocks.content:
Git is used everywhere in DAI starting Week 1.

- **Ubuntu / WSL:** `sudo apt install git`
- **macOS:** `brew install git` — **Important:** macOS ships a pre-installed Git with Apple developer tools, but it is usually several versions behind. Always prefer Homebrew's up-to-date `git`.

Next, configure your global Git identity. Git stamps this name and email onto every commit you create:

```bash
git config --global user.name "First-name Last-name"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"
```

> **Note:** `user.name` and `user.email` are just a label, not cryptographic proof of authorship. You will configure SSH keys and **cryptographically signed commits** in Chapter 02.

Finally, create a **GitHub** account using an email address you will keep after your studies—your repositories will become part of your developer portfolio.

sections.title: 5. Java 25 LTS, Maven (via SDKMAN!) & IntelliJ IDEA
sections.description: Install the Java toolchain cleanly with SDKMAN!, connect IntelliJ IDEA to WSL2 on Windows, and synthesize your setup knowledge.

blocks.title: Installing Java 25 LTS & Maven with SDKMAN!
blocks.content:
**SDKMAN!** manages Java toolchain versions cleanly, letting you install and switch between JDKs without manual `PATH` or `JAVA_HOME` edits.

1. Install SDKMAN! following the `curl` command at https://sdkman.io/, then **open a new terminal** (if SDKMAN! complains about missing packages like `zip`/`unzip` on Ubuntu/WSL, install them with `sudo apt install <package>` and retry).
2. Install the latest **Temurin** LTS Java (Java 25 at the time of writing) and **Maven**:

```bash
sdk list java
sdk install java <version>-tem
sdk install maven
```

3. Verify all three tools in your Unix terminal:
   - `sdk version`
   - `java --version` (should show Temurin 25 or newer LTS)
   - `mvn --version` (should show Maven running on that Java)

blocks.title: IntelliJ IDEA & Windows-to-WSL2 Integration
blocks.content:
**IntelliJ IDEA** is the supported IDE for DAI (Community or Ultimate—no Ultimate-only features are used; you can optionally activate a free JetBrains student license with your HEIG-VD email). Install it via the **JetBrains Toolbox App** (on Windows, install Toolbox on **Windows**, *not* inside WSL).

### Windows-Only: Connect IntelliJ to WSL2

1. Allow WSL through the Windows Firewall in an **Administrator PowerShell**:

```powershell
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "WSL" -Direction Inbound -InterfaceAlias "vEthernet (WSL (Hyper-V firewall))" -Action Allow
Get-NetFirewallProfile -Name Public | Get-NetFirewallRule | where DisplayName -ILike "IntelliJ IDEA*" | Disable-NetFirewallRule
```

2. **Two Golden Rules for the Semester:**
   - **Rule 1:** Create all projects in your WSL home directory (`\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-<version>\home\<user>`), never on the Windows side.
   - **Rule 2:** IntelliJ's built-in terminal must open WSL, not PowerShell. If it opens PowerShell, go to **Settings > Tools > Terminal** and set the shell path to `wsl.exe -d Ubuntu-<your-version>`.

> **Troubleshooting:** If IntelliJ cannot find Java or Maven inside WSL, double-check the **Windows Defender exclusion** (`Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath '\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-<your-version>'`)—it is the most common blocker.

blocks.title: Complete Week-1 Environment Verification Script
blocks.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
cat /etc/os-release | head -n 2
apt --version || brew --version
git --version
git config user.name
sdk version
java --version
mvn --version

annotations.note: On WSL2/Ubuntu, confirms your Ubuntu LTS distribution version.
Confirms your Git commit author label is configured.
Must report Temurin 25 (or newer LTS) managed by SDKMAN!.
Verifies Maven is installed and bound to the same Java 25 runtime.

blocks.title: Synthesis: Diagnosing a Broken Windows WSL2 + IntelliJ Setup
blocks.prompt: A classmate on Windows reports two problems: (1) their Maven builds are painfully slow and file permissions keep breaking because they created their project in C:\Users\Alex\DAI, and (2) when they move the project to WSL, IntelliJ IDEA still cannot detect Java 25 or Maven inside Ubuntu. Diagnose both issues and write out the exact fixes.
self_check_criteria: Identified that storing projects on C:\ (/mnt/c/) crosses the Windows-Linux filesystem boundary, causing slow I/O and permission issues.
Specified moving projects into the WSL Linux home directory (/home/<user>, accessed via \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-<version>\home\<user>).
Identified Windows Defender scanning \\wsl.localhost\... as the primary blocker for IntelliJ detecting Java/Maven in WSL.
Mentioned checking Windows Firewall rules for vEthernet (WSL) and setting IntelliJ's terminal to wsl.exe -d Ubuntu-<version>.
blocks.model_answer:
1) Storing projects in C:\Users\Alex\DAI forces WSL2 to access files across the 9P Windows-Linux bridge (/mnt/c/), which is much slower and breaks Unix file permissions. The fix is to create and store all projects inside the Ubuntu home directory (/home/<user>, opened in IntelliJ via \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-<version>\home\<user>) and never edit them from Windows File Explorer.

2) When IntelliJ cannot detect Java 25 or Maven inside WSL, the most common culprit is Windows Defender blocking/throttling \\wsl.localhost. Running `Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath '\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-<your-version>'` in an Administrator PowerShell (along with enabling the WSL Hyper-V firewall rule) resolves the detection issue. Also verify IntelliJ's built-in terminal is set to `wsl.exe -d Ubuntu-<your-version>`.

blocks.target_audience: a first-year student who has only ever used Windows File Explorer
blocks.prompt: Explain in plain language why WSL2 has two separate file worlds (/home/<user> vs /mnt/c/), and why putting Java projects in C:\ or dragging files with Windows File Explorer causes trouble.
key_points_to_cover: WSL2 runs a real Linux computer inside Windows with its own native Linux disk (/home/<user>).
Accessing C:\ (/mnt/c/) or poking into Linux files from Windows Explorer forces two different operating systems to translate permissions and file formats across a slow bridge.
Keeping projects in /home/<user> and using only the Ubuntu terminal and IntelliJ avoids permission corruption and slow builds.

sections.title: 6. Knowledge Retrieval & Spaced Repetition
sections.description: Test your understanding of DAI's course structure, grading math, and environment setup with diagnostic questions and flashcards.

blocks.title: Compute the Final DAI Grade
blocks.question: A student scores **TE1 = 4.0**, **TE2 = 5.0**, and **PW = 5.5**. Using the DAI grading formula $(\text{TE1} \times 0.4 + \text{TE2} \times 0.6) \times 0.8 + \text{PW} \times 0.2$, what is their final grade?
blocks.explanation:
First compute the cours average: $4.0 \times 0.4 + 5.0 \times 0.6 = 1.6 + 3.0 = 4.6$. Next, weight cours at 80% and PW at 20%: $(4.6 \times 0.8) + (5.5 \times 0.2) = 3.68 + 1.10 = 4.78$.

* '4.62' reverses the TE1 and TE2 weights ($4.0 \times 0.6 + 5.0 \times 0.4 = 4.4$, then $4.4 \times 0.8 + 5.5 \times 0.2 = 4.62$).
* '4.83' is an unweighted simple average $(4.0 + 5.0 + 5.5) / 3$.
* '3.68' forgets to add the `PW * 0.2` term.
hints: Start inside the parentheses: compute the weighted cours average using 0.4 for TE1 and 0.6 for TE2.
Multiply the cours average by 0.8, then add 20% of the PW grade (5.5 × 0.2).

blocks.title: DAI Course Structure & Logistics
blocks.question: Which of the following statements about how DAI operates are **true**? (Select all that apply)
options: All course communication and Q&A happen on GitHub Discussions rather than Cyberlearn or Teams.
There is no final exam session; all evaluations happen during the semester.
Course material is written in English, while classes and evaluations are in French.
The "Go further" sections in chapters are mandatory and tested on TE1 and TE2.
correct_answer: All course communication and Q&A happen on GitHub Discussions rather than Cyberlearn or Teams.
There is no final exam session; all evaluations happen during the semester.
Course material is written in English, while classes and evaluations are in French.
blocks.explanation: DAI uses GitHub Discussions exclusively for communication, has no exam session (grading is strictly TE1, TE2, and 3 PWs during the semester), and pairs English chapters with French classes/evaluations. However, the collapsible 'Go further' boxes are optional enrichment for the curious—evaluations only cover the core chapter content.
hints: Check Chapter 01's 'How the course works' section regarding communication channels and languages.
Recall what evaluations cover: core chapter content vs. collapsible 'Go further' boxes.

blocks.title: WSL2 Project Storage & File Access
blocks.question: On Windows with WSL2, where should you store your DAI Java projects, and how should you manipulate those files?
options: Store them in `/home/<user>` (inside WSL) and manipulate them only from the Ubuntu terminal or IntelliJ.
Store them in `C:\Users\<user>\Projects` (`/mnt/c/...`) so both Windows Explorer and Ubuntu can edit them freely.
Store them in `/home/<user>` and regularly organize or rename them using Windows File Explorer at `\\wsl.localhost\...`.
Use Git Bash on Windows so all files stay native to `C:\` without needing WSL2.
blocks.correct_answer: Store them in `/home/<user>` (inside WSL) and manipulate them only from the Ubuntu terminal or IntelliJ.
blocks.explanation: All projects must live in the Linux home directory (`/home/<user>`, shorthand `~`) and be manipulated only via the Ubuntu terminal or IntelliJ. Storing projects under `/mnt/c/` causes slow cross-OS I/O, while editing WSL files from Windows File Explorer causes permission issues and odd file behaviors. Git Bash is explicitly unsupported.
hints: Think about which filesystem is native to the Ubuntu terminal where your builds and Docker containers run.
Recall the Caution box in Chapter 00 about mixing Windows File Explorer with WSL files.

blocks.title: Print Working Directory Command
blocks.question: In a Unix terminal, the ___ command prints the full path of your current working directory.
blocks.explanation: `pwd` stands for 'print working directory' and outputs the absolute path of the folder your shell is currently in. `ls` lists directory contents, `cd` changes directories, and `cat` prints file contents.
hints: It is a 3-letter acronym for 'Print Working Directory'.
In Unix shells, it tells you where `cd` has currently placed you.

blocks.title: Git Installation on macOS
blocks.question: Why does Chapter 00 instruct macOS users to run `brew install git` even though macOS already ships a `git` binary with Apple developer tools?
options: Apple's pre-installed Git is usually several versions behind, so Homebrew provides an up-to-date version.
Apple's pre-installed Git cannot connect to GitHub over HTTPS.
Homebrew's Git automatically generates SSH keys and GPG commit signatures.
Apple's Git only works inside IntelliJ IDEA and cannot run in the terminal.
blocks.correct_answer: Apple's pre-installed Git is usually several versions behind, so Homebrew provides an up-to-date version.
blocks.explanation: macOS ships a Git binary with Apple's Command Line Tools, but it lags several versions behind upstream Git releases. Installing via `brew install git` ensures you have a modern, up-to-date Git. Neither version auto-generates SSH/GPG signatures (that's covered in Chapter 02).
hints: Check the comment in the macOS Git installation snippet in Chapter 00.
It is about software freshness/versioning rather than missing protocol support.

blocks.title: Predict Output: Grade Calculation Snippet
blocks.explanation:
Compute `cours`: `5.0 * 0.4 + 4.0 * 0.6 = 2.0 + 2.4 = 4.4`. Then compute `finalGrade`: `4.4 * 0.8 + 6.0 * 0.2 = 3.52 + 1.20 = 4.72`.

* '4.88' swaps the TE1 and TE2 weights (`5.0 * 0.6 + 4.0 * 0.4 = 4.6`, `4.6 * 0.8 + 1.2 = 4.88`).
* '5.00' is the unweighted average `(5 + 4 + 6) / 3`.
* '4.56' mistakenly applies `0.2` to `cours` or miscalculates `3.52 + 1.04`.
hints: Compute `cours` first: `5.0 * 0.4` is `2.0`, and `4.0 * 0.6` is `2.4`.

blocks.title: Troubleshooting IntelliJ IDEA + WSL2 on Windows
blocks.question: A Windows student installed Java 25 and Maven via SDKMAN! inside Ubuntu WSL2, but IntelliJ IDEA cannot detect them and its built-in terminal opens PowerShell. Which actions are part of the official Chapter 00 fix? (Select all that apply)
options: Add a Windows Defender exclusion for `\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-<your-version>` in an Administrator PowerShell.
Add an inbound Windows Firewall allow rule for `vEthernet (WSL (Hyper-V firewall))`.
Set IntelliJ's Terminal shell path to `wsl.exe -d Ubuntu-<your-version>` in Settings > Tools > Terminal.
Install a second copy of JetBrains Toolbox inside Ubuntu WSL2 and launch IntelliJ from there.
correct_answer: Add a Windows Defender exclusion for `\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-<your-version>` in an Administrator PowerShell.
Add an inbound Windows Firewall allow rule for `vEthernet (WSL (Hyper-V firewall))`.
Set IntelliJ's Terminal shell path to `wsl.exe -d Ubuntu-<your-version>` in Settings > Tools > Terminal.
blocks.explanation: Chapter 00 explicitly instructs Windows users to: (1) exclude `\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-<your-version>` in Windows Defender (a known blocker for IntelliJ finding Java/Maven in WSL), (2) allow `vEthernet (WSL (Hyper-V firewall))` in Windows Firewall, and (3) set IntelliJ's Terminal shell path to `wsl.exe -d Ubuntu-<your-version>`. JetBrains Toolbox must be installed on Windows, *not* inside WSL.
hints: Recall the Windows-only IntelliJ + WSL integration section in Chapter 00.
Where should JetBrains Toolbox be installed on Windows?

blocks.title: DAI AI Tools Accountability Rule
blocks.question: According to Chapter 01's AI tools policy, what is the core test of whether you used an AI assistant responsibly on a lab or practical work?
options: You can explain every line of the submitted code yourself, because evaluations happen without AI.
You disclose the AI model name in your README, which exempts you from explaining the code.
You only use AI for comments and documentation, never for debugging errors.
AI assistants are completely banned from all labs and practical works.
blocks.correct_answer: You can explain every line of the submitted code yourself, because evaluations happen without AI.
blocks.explanation:
DAI allows responsible AI use to understand errors or explore approaches, with one strict rule: if you cannot explain your code line by line, it is not your code. Since TE1 and TE2 happen without AI, outsourcing your learning is self-defeating.

* Disclosing the AI model in a README never exempts you from accountability for every line you submit.
* AI is explicitly allowed for understanding errors/debugging (not restricted to comments only).
* AI is not banned from labs/PWs—it is permitted with responsibility, though banned during evaluations.
hints: Re-read the three bullet points under 'AI tools' in Chapter 01.
Remember why evaluations (TE1/TE2) matter for your lab/PW workflow.

blocks.title: DAI Final Grade Formula
blocks.front: What is the exact **DAI final grade formula**, and what is the effective weight of TE1, TE2, and PW?
blocks.back:
$$\text{final grade} = (\text{TE1} \times 0.4 + \text{TE2} \times 0.6) \times 0.8 + \text{PW} \times 0.2$$

- **TE1:** $32\%$ ($0.4 \times 0.8$)
- **TE2:** $48\%$ ($0.6 \times 0.8$)
- **PW (avg of 3):** $20\%$
- **No exam session**—everything happens during the semester.
blocks.hint: 80% cours (split 40/60 between TE1 and TE2) + 20% labo (PW).

blocks.title: WSL2 Home (~) vs Windows Mount (/mnt/c/)
blocks.front: In WSL2, what is the difference between `/home/<user>` (`~`) and `/mnt/c/`, and where must DAI projects live?
blocks.back:
- **`/home/<user>` (`~`):** Your native Linux home directory inside WSL2. **All DAI projects must live here.**
- **`/mnt/c/`:** Cross-OS mount of your Windows `C:\` drive.
- Never edit WSL project files from Windows File Explorer (`\\wsl.localhost\...`), as it causes permission issues and odd file behaviors.
blocks.hint: One is native Linux storage; the other crosses an OS bridge.

blocks.title: SDKMAN! Java 25 LTS & Maven Commands
blocks.front: How do you list, install, and verify **Temurin Java 25 LTS** and **Maven** using **SDKMAN!**?
blocks.back:
1. `sdk list java` (find latest `<version>-tem` LTS)
2. `sdk install java <version>-tem`
3. `sdk install maven`
4. Verify with `sdk version`, `java --version`, and `mvn --version`.

blocks.title: Core Unix Terminal Commands
blocks.front: What do `pwd`, `touch`, `rm -r`, `cp -r`, `less`, and `tail -f` do in a Unix shell?
blocks.back:
- `pwd`: Print working directory
- `touch <file>`: Create empty file
- `rm -r <dir>`: Recursively delete directory
- `cp -r <src> <dst>`: Recursively copy directory
- `less <file>`: Page through file (`q` to quit)
- `tail -f <file>`: Follow live lines (e.g., logs)
blocks.hint: Basic file navigation, creation, deletion, and log inspection.

blocks.title: Git Global Identity Configuration
blocks.front: How do you set your Git author name and email globally, and is this a cryptographic proof of identity?
blocks.back:
```bash
git config --global user.name "First-name Last-name"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"
```
No—it is only a **label** stamped on commits. Cryptographic commit signing is configured in Chapter 02.

blocks.title: DAI AI Tools Ground Rules
blocks.front: What are the **three ground rules** for using AI assistants (Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude) in DAI?
blocks.back:
1. Use AI to **understand** (explain errors, explore approaches), not to generate work you cannot explain.
2. **Accountability:** If you cannot explain your code line by line, it is not your code.
3. **Evaluations (TE1/TE2) have no AI**—outsourcing learning will show there.

blocks.title: Two Golden Rules for IntelliJ + WSL2
blocks.front: What are the **two rules** every Windows student must respect for IntelliJ IDEA all semester?
blocks.back:
1. Create all projects in your **WSL home** (`\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-<version>\home\<user>`), never on the Windows side.
2. Set IntelliJ's built-in terminal to open **WSL** (`wsl.exe -d Ubuntu-<your-version>`), not PowerShell.
blocks.hint: Project location + built-in terminal shell path.
